Batch dropper spawns hidden PowerShell pulling installer.exe from pixeldrain.com AIInstallation High
Detects the execution stage: cmd/batch spawning a hidden PowerShell that downloads installer.exe from pixeldrain.com into %TEMP%, runs it silently, then self-deletes. Article-specific because pixeldrain.com in a script command line is the exact final-payload retrieval host Microsoft published. Rationale: pixeldrain.com in a scripting-host command line is the exact final-installer retrieval Microsoft and the second-source write-up documented; it is rare enough in enterprise scripting to alert on directly, and the cmd->hidden-powershell->pixeldrain->self-delete chain matches the published behavior precisely. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/ • https://windowsnews.ai/article/a-phishing-empire-fell-and-now-the-calls-are-coming-inside-microsofts-q2-2026-security-shakeup.440163
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1105 T1564.003 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer or researcher legitimately using curl/PowerShell to fetch a file shared via pixeldrain.com
  • Security analyst manually reproducing the download in an isolated VM
  • A CI/automation script pulling an artifact from a pixeldrain link
  • Rare power-user using pixeldrain as personal file transfer over corporate device
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe","devenv.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the full command line and parent process — confirm parent is cmd.exe running a .bat and the child is hidden-window PowerShell/curl; check for installer.exe written to the user's Temp. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the process tree, capture installer.exe (or its FileWritten hash before self-delete) for analysis, and block pixeldrain.com egress. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep the fleet for the same pixeldrain.com command-line pattern and for the delivery IOCs (UC-1 sender, UC-2 clickup .bat) to scope other recipients who executed.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "pixeldrain.com"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| extend HiddenOrTemp = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-w hidden","-windowstyle hidden","hidden","-nop","-noprofile","\\Temp\\","installer.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, HiddenOrTemp, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "pixeldrain.com"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Script host downloading installer.exe from pixeldrain.com
id: c19a7e30-4b6d-4c22-8f7e-1a2b3c4d5e6f
description: Detects powershell/cmd/curl referencing pixeldrain.com in the command line, matching the Q2 2026 Microsoft-documented final-payload retrieval (installer.exe to %TEMP%, silent run, dropper self-delete).
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

logsource:

detection:

      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @CommandLine:*pixeldrain.com* @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\CMD.EXE OR *\\curl.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/pixeldrain\.com/i
| ImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh|cmd|curl)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*pixeldrain.com*" AND (Processes.process_name="powershell.exe" OR Processes.process_name="pwsh.exe" OR Processes.process_name="cmd.exe" OR Processes.process_name="curl.exe") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*pixeldrain.com*" AND (Processes.process_name="powershell.exe" OR Processes.process_name="pwsh.exe" OR Processes.process_name="cmd.exe" OR Processes.process_name="curl.exe") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Endpoint network/DNS egress to pixeldrain.com from a LOLBin / script host AICommand & Control Medium
Network-telemetry safety-net for the final payload retrieval: any host resolving/connecting to pixeldrain.com, especially initiated by a scripting host or LOLBin rather than a browser. Catches the download even when command-line auditing is disabled and the dropper name varies. Rationale: pixeldrain.com is the named final-payload host (table 1 URL hxxps://pixeldrain[.]com/api/file/3v92oJiL) and is uncommon in corporate traffic; scoping the initiator to LOLBins/script hosts keeps it high-signal while surviving cases where command-line logging (UC-3) is off. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/ • https://any.run/report/84f73741867e012140103aa9eb59bfaef6bf8c02aa7b9579be7aad2143418c03/18abf34d-1f07-4902-8343-13b9f8358605
ATT&CKT1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately downloading a file someone shared via pixeldrain in a browser (excluded by the LOLBin initiator filter in Defender, but DNS-only sources will still see it)
  • Researcher/sandbox pulling samples from pixeldrain
  • Security tooling enriching pixeldrain IOCs by resolving the domain
  • curl/PowerShell used by a developer to fetch a legitimately shared artifact
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process — a browser is likely benign, but powershell/cmd/curl/certutil to pixeldrain is high-priority; correlate with any installer.exe write in %TEMP% on the same host. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host if a script host initiated the connection, block pixeldrain.com at the egress proxy/DNS, and collect the downloaded binary. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot the host and user back to UC-1 (campaign email) and UC-2 (clickup .bat) to confirm the full chain and identify other victims resolving pixeldrain.com in the same window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "pixeldrain.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "pixeldrain.com"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, IPAddresses = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/24

logsource:

  product: windows
detection:

    QueryName|contains: 'pixeldrain.com'
  condition: selection

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationHostname:*pixeldrain.com* @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\certutil.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/pixeldrain\.com/i

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution where DNS.query="*pixeldrain.com*" by DNS.src, DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email

         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject

     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

Auth.js v5 fail-open trigger: server-configuration error emitted in app logs AIExploitation High
Hunts the exact Auth.js/next-auth v5 configuration-error log lines (InvalidEndpoints, MissingSecret/AUTH_SECRET, or the generic 'problem with the server configuration' message) that flip the auth() wrapper into returning a truthy error object instead of null. Once this appears, any middleware using existence-only checks (!!auth / if(req.auth)) fails open and treats every request as authenticated. Rationale: Uses the advisory's verbatim strings: the '[auth][error]' prefix, the named error classes 'InvalidEndpoints' and 'MissingSecret'/'AUTH_SECRET', and the surfaced message 'problem with the server configuration'. These are high-fidelity because they are Auth.js internal error identifiers that appear only when the configuration breaks — the precise precondition for the fail-open state. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8fpg-xm3f-6cx3 • https://authjs.dev/reference/core/errors • https://authjs.dev/getting-started/session-management/protecting
ATT&CKT1556
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Transient config error during a rolling deploy that is corrected within seconds (env var briefly unset)
  • Non-production/staging hosts intentionally running with an incomplete provider config
  • A monitoring or documentation tool echoing the error text back into logs
  • Local developer environment logs shipped to the same index
  • Deliberate chaos/DR testing of the auth layer
Suppression filter
| where Computer !has "staging" and Computer !has "dev" and HostName !has "preview"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the app is on a vulnerable next-auth build (>=5.0.0-beta.0, <=5.0.0-beta.31) and that middleware uses existence-only checks (!!auth / if(req.auth)) rather than !!req.auth?.user; identify the affected host/environment and whether it is internet-facing. 2) CONTAIN: Restore the missing env var (AUTH_SECRET / provider issuer|authorization) or roll back the deploy; if it is production and internet-facing, gate traffic at the LB until fixed and apply the documented workaround (check req.auth?.user). 3) HUNT: Pull access logs for the error window and look for successful (200/302) requests to protected routes from sessions with no auth cookie — pivot to UC 'Auth.js fail-open: protected-route access during a config-error window'.
// Auth.js config-error state that causes existence-based auth checks to fail open
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SyslogMessage has "[auth][error]"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("InvalidEndpoints", "MissingSecret", "AUTH_SECRET", "problem with the server configuration")
| summarize ErrorCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleLog = any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, HostName, ProcessName
| order by LastSeen desc
title: Auth.js v5 Fail-Open Configuration Error (InvalidEndpoints / MissingSecret)
id: a4dbb25b-f4c7-5bdd-af42-49468d365b01
description: Detects Auth.js (next-auth v5) server-configuration errors that cause the auth() wrapper to return a truthy error object, making existence-based auth checks fail open (GHSA-8fpg-xm3f-6cx3).
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8fpg-xm3f-6cx3
  - https://authjs.dev/reference/core/errors
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/24
tags:
  - attack.t1556
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  product: nodejs
  service: application
detection:
  selection_prefix:
    keywords:
      - '[auth][error]'
  selection_error:
    keywords:
      - 'InvalidEndpoints'
      - 'MissingSecret'
      - 'AUTH_SECRET'
      - 'problem with the server configuration'
  condition: selection_prefix and selection_error
level: high
"[auth][error]" AND ("InvalidEndpoints" OR "MissingSecret" OR "AUTH_SECRET" OR "problem with the server configuration")
# log group: /aws/lambda/<your-nextjs-app>  (or the ECS/app-runner app log group hosting Auth.js)
fields @timestamp, @logStream, @message
| filter @message like /\[auth\]\[error\]/ and @message like /(InvalidEndpoints|MissingSecret|AUTH_SECRET|problem with the server configuration)/
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 200
APPLICATION
index=* ("[auth][error]") ("InvalidEndpoints" OR "MissingSecret" OR "AUTH_SECRET" OR "problem with the server configuration")
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(_raw) as sampleLog by host, source, sourcetype
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - count
Auth.js fail-open: protected-route access succeeds during a config-error window AIExploitation Medium
Correlates Auth.js '[auth][error]' log lines with successful (200/302) HTTP responses to protected application routes in the same short time window. During the config-error state the auth object is truthy for everyone, so unauthenticated requests to gated routes start returning success instead of redirect/401 — this catches the bypass being exercised, not just the enabling condition. Rationale: Ties the advisory's cause ('[auth][error]' -> truthy auth object) to its observable effect (protected routes returning 200/302 to requests that should have been denied). Scoping to /api/ excluding /api/auth targets application-protected routes without a customer-specific placeholder; the AnonReqs/empty-username count highlights sessions that succeeded without an authenticated user. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8fpg-xm3f-6cx3 • https://authjs.dev/getting-started/session-management/protecting
ATT&CKT1556 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuinely public /api routes that are intentionally unauthenticated (health, webhooks, public content)
  • Config error and legitimate authenticated traffic simply coinciding in the same 5-minute bin
  • API routes that perform their own token/role check downstream and are not gated by the vulnerable middleware
  • Load-balancer or uptime-probe hitting API endpoints during the error window
  • Static/cached responses served without hitting the auth middleware
Suppression filter
| where not(CsUriStem in ("/api/health", "/api/healthz", "/api/ping", "/api/webhooks"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For each flagged bin, pull the individual AppServiceHTTPLogs rows and check whether the succeeding requests carried a valid session cookie / CsUsername — no-cookie 200s to a gated route during an error window are true positives. 2) CONTAIN: Fix the underlying config (restore AUTH_SECRET / provider endpoints) or roll back; treat any data returned to unauthenticated callers as potentially exposed and revoke/rotate as needed. 3) HUNT: Enumerate every distinct source IP and path served during the window, and search for follow-on actions (data reads, privileged API calls) from those IPs after the fail-open period.
// Successful protected-route access occurring in the same 5-min bin as an Auth.js config error = fail-open exercised
let ErrBins = Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where SyslogMessage has "[auth][error]"
    | extend Bin = bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
    | distinct Bin;
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ScStatus in (200, 302)
| where CsUriStem startswith "/api/" and not(CsUriStem startswith "/api/auth")
| extend Bin = bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| join kind=inner (ErrBins) on Bin
| summarize Requests = count(), Paths = make_set(CsUriStem, 20), SourceIPs = make_set(CIp, 50), AnonReqs = countif(isempty(CsUsername)) by Bin, CsHost
| order by Bin desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web where Web.status IN ("200","302") Web.url="/api/*" NOT Web.url="/api/auth*" by _time span=5m, Web.site, Web.src, Web.url, Web.status
| rename Web.* as *
| join type=inner _time [
    search index=* "[auth][error]"
    | bin _time span=5m
    | stats count as authErrors by _time ]
| where authErrors > 0
| stats sum(count) as okProtectedReqs values(url) as urls values(src) as sourceIPs by _time, site
| sort - _time
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.status IN ("200","302") Web.url="/api/*" NOT Web.url="/api/auth*" by _time span=5m, Web.site, Web.src, Web.url, Web.status
| rename Web.* as *
| join type=inner _time [
    search index=* "[auth][error]"
    | bin _time span=5m
    | stats count as authErrors by _time ]
| where authErrors > 0
| stats sum(count) as okProtectedReqs values(url) as urls values(src) as sourceIPs by _time, site
| sort - _time
Auth.js: protected /api access returning success with no session cookie (fail-open evidence) AIExploitation Medium
Standalone hunt for the observable outcome of the bypass: successful (200/302) responses to protected application routes where the request carried NO Auth.js session cookie (authjs.session-token / __Secure-authjs.session-token). Under the vulnerable existence-only check, an unauthenticated request with no session cookie is granted access — this surfaces that outcome even without pairing to the error log. Rationale: Grounded in the advisory's core claim that access is granted to 'every request, including unauthenticated ones', combined with the known Auth.js v5 default session-cookie name 'authjs.session-token' (and its '__Secure-' HTTPS variant). A gated /api route returning 200/302 to a request with no session cookie and no authenticated user is the direct fingerprint of the fail-open. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8fpg-xm3f-6cx3 • https://authjs.dev/getting-started/session-management/protecting
ATT&CKT1078 T1556
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimately public /api endpoints that never require a session (health, public config, webhooks)
  • First request of a login flow before any session cookie is set
  • API keys / bearer-token auth used instead of session cookies (auth carried in Authorization header, not the cookie)
  • Access logs that do not capture the Cookie header, causing every row to look cookie-less
  • CDN/edge-cached API responses served without the origin auth middleware
Suppression filter
| where not(CsUriStem in ("/api/health", "/api/healthz", "/api/ping", "/api/webhooks", "/api/public"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the flagged /api paths are actually meant to be authenticated (not public); check whether auth is expected via Authorization header rather than cookie before calling it a bypass. 2) CONTAIN: If confirmed, apply the Auth.js fix/workaround (check req.auth?.user, restore config) and revoke exposure; block the offending source IPs if abuse is evident. 3) HUNT: Cross-reference these no-cookie successes against '[auth][error]' log windows to confirm causation, and review what data/actions those requests obtained to scope the exposure.
// Protected /api routes returning success to a request that carried NO Auth.js session cookie
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ScStatus in (200, 302)
| where CsUriStem startswith "/api/" and not(CsUriStem startswith "/api/auth")
| where isempty(Cookie) or Cookie !contains "authjs.session-token"
| where isempty(CsUsername)
| summarize Requests = count(), Paths = make_set(CsUriStem, 20), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by CsHost, CIp
| where Requests > 0
| order by LastSeen desc
CLOUD
index=* sourcetype=*:access* (status=200 OR status=302) uri_path="/api/*" NOT uri_path="/api/auth*" NOT cookie="*authjs.session-token*"
| stats count as reqs values(uri_path) as paths dc(src_ip) as srcIPs by host, src_ip
| where reqs > 0
| sort - reqs

CL-STA-1114 (Void Blizzard) Zimbra espionage C2/exfil infrastructure contact AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any host resolving or connecting to the nine hard-coded C2 domains or nine C2 IPs used by CL-STA-1114 / Void Blizzard to receive stolen Zimbra webmail data (credentials, 2FA scratch codes, CSRF tokens, 90-day mail archive). Article-specific because it matches the exact IOC set Unit 42 attributes to this campaign, not a generic beacon shape. Rationale: Uses the exact nine C2 domains and nine C2 IPs Unit 42 attributes to CL-STA-1114; cross-checked against CISA AA26-204A and The Hacker News which independently confirm the Void Blizzard/LAUNDRY BEAR Zimbra campaign, so the IOCs meet the two-source bar. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa26-204a • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/russian-espionage-group-exploited.html • https://cyberscoop.com/russian-laundry-bear-zimbra-exploit/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel platform or sandbox detonating the same IOCs from a research host
  • Security scanner / EDR retro-hunt actively probing the IOC list
  • DNS sinkhole or protective-DNS appliance logging the resolution before blocking
  • A legitimately-registered look-alike domain reclaimed post-takedown resolving to benign parking infrastructure
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host and the initiating process (browser vs. service); confirm the user has an active Zimbra webmail session and whether the org runs unpatched ZCS (<10.0.18 / <10.1.13). 2) Contain: block all nine domains/IPs at proxy+DNS, isolate the host, and force-reset the affected user's Zimbra password and 2FA scratch codes (the payload steals both). 3) Hunt: pivot on the user/device for the last 90 days of mailbox access, search all endpoints for any of the nine IOCs, and review Zimbra logs for the CSS @import XSS mail that triggered it.

Inbound HTML-attachment lure exploiting Zimbra XSS (CVE-2025-66376) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound emails delivered with an HTML/HTM attachment (or news-headline lure body) to webmail users — the CL-STA-1114 delivery vector that carries the obfuscated Base64/SVG payload abusing Zimbra's CSS @import XSS. Article-specific in that it targets the zero-click HTML-borne exploit rather than generic malicious attachments. Rationale: Article states initial access is a phishing email with an HTML attachment or embedded HTML carrying the Base64/SVG payload; corroborating CISA/SentinelOne detail confirms CVE-2025-66376 fires on viewing crafted HTML mail, so inbound HTML attachments to webmail users are the delivery pivot. Kept as hunting given benign HTML attachments are common. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2025-66376/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa26-204a
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1203
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Marketing/newsletter platforms that send rich HTML as an attachment
  • Automated report/invoice systems delivering .htm exports
  • Internal ticketing or monitoring tools emailing HTML dashboards inbound via a relay
  • Recruiter/CV emails with HTML resumes
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromDomain !in~ ("news.example-vendor.com") and not (SenderMailFromDomain endswith "mailchimpapp.net")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the HTML attachment in a sandbox and grep for CSS @import, invisible <svg onload>, atob()/Base64 blobs, or references to the nine campaign domains. 2) Contain: if malicious, purge the message tenant-wide (soft-delete), block sender + any embedded domain, and reset the recipient's Zimbra credentials and 2FA scratch codes. 3) Hunt: confirm whether the org runs unpatched ZCS, and correlate the recipient against the C2-contact detection to see if exfiltration already occurred.
EmailAttachmentInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileType in~ ("html","htm")
| join kind=inner (
    EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
    | where DeliveryAction in ("Delivered","DeliveredAsSpam")
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, FileName, FileType, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, ThreatTypes
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailAttachmentInfo
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where FileType in~ ("html","htm")
| join kind=inner (
    EmailEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
    | where DeliveryAction in ("Delivered","DeliveredAsSpam")
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, FileName, FileType, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, ThreatTypes
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Browser-initiated webmail data exfiltration to CL-STA-1114 C2 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a browser process (the authenticated Zimbra session) making outbound HTTP connections to the campaign's C2 domains/IPs — the moment the injected JavaScript ships stolen credentials, 2FA scratch codes, CSRF tokens and mail archive off-box. Distinct from the broad C2 detection by requiring a browser initiator and HTTP egress shape. Rationale: Combines the campaign's confirmed C2 IOC set with a browser-process initiator, because the CVE-2025-66376 XSS runs inside the authenticated Zimbra browser session and the injected JS exfiltrates over HTTP — a browser hitting these specific hosts is high-fidelity exfil, not generic web traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa26-204a • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/russian-espionage-group-exploited.html
ATT&CKT1041 T1539 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst manually browsing to a seized/sinkholed C2 domain during investigation
  • Browser prefetch/DNS-preconnect to a domain reclaimed post-takedown
  • URL-reputation browser extension pinging a look-alike domain
  • Sandbox/detonation VM using a real browser to detonate the sample
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--headless" and DeviceName !in~ ("SANDBOX-DETONATE01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the browser had an active Zimbra session and inspect the request (POST body size, user-agent) for outbound credential/mail data. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the C2 at proxy+DNS, and immediately reset the user's Zimbra password, 2FA scratch codes, and invalidate active sessions/CSRF tokens. 3) Hunt: sweep all browsers org-wide for the nine IOCs, review the mailbox for 90-day access anomalies, and check whether the org's ZCS is unpatched.

Unpatched Zimbra Collaboration exposed to CVE-2025-66376 (Void Blizzard target) AIExploitation High
Surfaces endpoints/servers running Zimbra Collaboration versions vulnerable to CVE-2025-66376 — the CSS @import stored-XSS that CL-STA-1114 exploits zero-click. Directly supports the article's proactive-patching guidance by listing exploitable ZCS instances (10.0<10.0.18, 10.1<10.1.13). Rationale: Uses the concrete CVE-2025-66376 identifier confirmed by SentinelOne's vuln database and the CISA advisory (affected 10.0<10.0.18 / 10.1<10.1.13); a TVM exposure hunt is the cleanest way to operationalize the article's patch-now message. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2025-66376/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-exploit-zimbra-zero-click-flaw-for-email-theft/
ATT&CKT1203 T1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • ZCS host already patched to 10.0.18/10.1.13 but TVM inventory lagging a scan cycle
  • Non-production/staging Zimbra instance not internet-exposed
  • Defender TVM mis-parsing a Zimbra build string on a Linux appliance
  • Decommissioned server still present in the device inventory
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the Zimbra build and whether the Classic Web Client (the vulnerable UI) is enabled and internet-reachable. 2) Contain: schedule emergency patch to 10.0.18 / 10.1.13, or disable the Classic UI / apply the vendor mitigation in the interim. 3) Hunt: on each exposed host, correlate against the C2-contact and browser-exfil detections and review Zimbra mail logs for crafted HTML messages abusing CSS @import.

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Claude Cowork Flaw Could Let AI Agent Escape Its VM and Access Mac Files

The Hacker News
2026-07-23 15 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have uncovered a sandbox escape vulnerability in Anthropic's Claude Cowork that makes it possible to break out of the confines of a Linux virtual machine (VM) within which the agent runs to read or write files anywhere on the Mac. Accomplish AI, which shared details of the vulnerability with The Hacker News ahead of publication, said about 500,000 macOS users running

CVEsCVE-2026-46331
ATT&CKT1021.001 T1190 T1195.002 T1486 T1528 T1555.003 T1566

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] CVE-2026-46331 pedit COW exploit: tc act_pedit action loaded on Cowork guest · [LLM] Cowork guest: unprivileged user + network namespace creation granting CAP_NET_ADMIN · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Cowork VM escape: guest process writing to host root via /mnt/.virtiofs-root · [LLM] Post-escape credential theft: Cowork guest reading host SSH/cloud keys via virtiofs mount · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Cowork VM escape: guest process writing to host root via /mnt/.virtiofs-root AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts any process inside the Claude Cowork Linux guest VM that reads or writes under the host-root virtiofs mount (/mnt/.virtiofs-root) — the exact path the SharedRoot escape uses to reach the Mac filesystem outside the connected folder. Only the coworkd root daemon should ever touch this mount; anything else is a post-exploit host breakout. Rationale: Uses the article's unique host-mount path /mnt/.virtiofs-root — only guest-root/coworkd should ever access it, so any other process touching it is the escape itself. Cross-checked against RHSB-2026-008 and gbhackers, which confirm the read-write host share as the escape vector. Cross-checked against: • https://access.redhat.com/security/vulnerabilities/RHSB-2026-008 • https://gbhackers.com/claude-cowork-sandbox-flaw/ • https://threat-modeling.com/anthropic-claude-cowork-sandbox-escape-root-access/
ATT&CKT1611 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • coworkd daemon performing its legitimate initial host-share mount (excluded by the coworkd filter)
  • Anthropic-shipped Cowork helper binaries enumerating the connected folder inside the mount
  • Backup or antivirus agent installed inside a custom VM image scanning /mnt
  • Admin manually mounting virtiofs for debugging a broken Cowork session (GitHub issue #25293/#26374 scenarios)
  • Cowork itself writing agent output back into the user-connected subfolder under the mount
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName != "coworkd" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "claude-cowork-helper"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is a macOS Cowork user running LOCAL (not cloud) execution, and identify the offending process (InitiatingProcessFileName/CommandLine) and which host paths outside the connected folder it touched. 2) Contain: kill the Cowork session/VM, switch the user to cloud-execution mode (the patched default), and rotate any credentials whose files sit under the accessed paths (~/.ssh, ~/.aws, keychain-adjacent files). 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for tc/act_pedit invocations and unprivileged user+net namespace creation (see companion UCs), and review /mnt/.virtiofs-root writes to system dirs (/etc, launch agents) for persistence.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath startswith "/mnt/.virtiofs-root/"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileDeleted")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName != "coworkd"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath startswith "/mnt/.virtiofs-root/"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileDeleted")
| where ActingProcessName !endswith "coworkd"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CVE-2026-46331 pedit COW exploit: tc act_pedit action loaded on Cowork guest AIExploitation High
Hunts execution of the iproute2 'tc' utility configuring an act_pedit action — the kernel path abused by CVE-2026-46331 (pedit COW) to gain guest-root inside the Cowork VM. Legitimate AI-agent workloads have no reason to program traffic-control packet editing, making tc+pedit a high-fidelity exploit signal. Rationale: act_pedit + tc is the exact kernel subsystem the article and RHSB-2026-008/TuxCare name for pedit COW; tc programming pedit actions never occurs in a normal AI-agent VM, so it is near-zero-noise evidence of CVE-2026-46331 exploitation. Cross-checked against: • https://access.redhat.com/security/vulnerabilities/RHSB-2026-008 • https://tuxcare.com/blog/pedit-cow-cve/ • https://canonical.com/blog/pedit-cow-linux-vulnerability-fixes-available
ATT&CKT1068 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Network/QoS engineers legitimately using tc pedit to rewrite DSCP/ToS bits on a router or gateway VM (not expected on a Cowork agent host)
  • Container/CNI tooling (some SDN plugins) programming tc actions at pod setup
  • tc traffic-shaping test scripts in a network lab image
  • Custom Cowork base image that ships a legitimate egress-shaping init script
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is a Cowork/agent VM where tc traffic-editing has no business running; capture the full tc command line and the invoking user (should be the disposable unprivileged session user). 2) Contain: terminate the session VM and block further local execution; force the affected user to cloud execution. Verify guest kernel is patched to >= v7.1-rc7 / distro-fixed build. 3) Hunt: on the same host correlate to preceding unprivileged user+net namespace creation and subsequent /mnt/.virtiofs-root writes, and check /bin/su for page-cache poisoning tampering.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName == "tc"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "pedit"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("action","filter","qdisc","add")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith "/tc" or TargetProcessName == "tc"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "pedit"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("action","filter","qdisc","add")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cowork guest: unprivileged user + network namespace creation granting CAP_NET_ADMIN AIExploitation Medium
Hunts creation of a combined user + network namespace by the disposable Cowork session user (via unshare or equivalent), the prerequisite that hands the session CAP_NET_ADMIN and makes the vulnerable tc/act_pedit path reachable in pedit COW. This is the 'namespaces make the privileged prerequisite available' step the researchers call out. Rationale: Directly encodes Hiltch's statement that user+network namespaces grant CAP_NET_ADMIN and expose the tc/act_pedit path; corroborated by RHSB-2026-008/Canonical noting unprivileged user namespaces as the exploit precondition. Medium confidence because container tooling also creates namespaces, so it is scoped to the user+net combination on agent hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://access.redhat.com/security/vulnerabilities/RHSB-2026-008 • https://canonical.com/blog/pedit-cow-linux-vulnerability-fixes-available
ATT&CKT1611 T1548
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rootless container runtimes (podman/buildah/nerdctl) legitimately unsharing user+net namespaces
  • Chrome/Electron sandbox launching via unshare inside the VM
  • CI/build tooling creating rootless namespaces
  • systemd-nspawn or bwrap-based sandboxes on a customized guest image
  • Developer manually testing namespace isolation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in ("podman","buildah","nerdctl","containerd","dockerd") and ProcessCommandLine !has "bwrap"
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the guest image legitimately runs rootless containers; if not, treat combined user+net namespace creation by the session user as suspicious and capture the full process tree. 2) Contain: end the session VM, move the user to cloud execution, and apply the mitigation of disabling unprivileged user namespaces (kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0) on locally-run guests. 3) Hunt: correlate within minutes to a following 'tc … pedit' invocation (UC2) and /mnt/.virtiofs-root writes (UC1) to confirm the full pedit COW chain rather than benign namespace use.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName == "unshare"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--user","--map-root-user","-U","-r") or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-[a-z]*U[a-z]*"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--net","-n") or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-[a-z]*n[a-z]*"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith "/unshare" or TargetProcessName == "unshare"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("--user","--map-root-user","-U","-r")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("--net","-n")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Post-escape credential theft: Cowork guest reading host SSH/cloud keys via virtiofs mount AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts commands inside the Cowork guest that read credential material (SSH keys, AWS/GCP/kube configs) through the host-root mount at /mnt/.virtiofs-root — the concrete impact the article warns of, where the escaped agent can harvest the Mac user's SSH keys and cloud credentials. Distinct from the generic escape signal by anchoring on sensitive credential paths beneath the mount. Rationale: Combines the article's unique host-mount path with the specific credential stores it names (SSH keys, cloud credentials); the pairing of /mnt/.virtiofs-root with .ssh/.aws/.kube in one command line is unambiguous credential theft through the escaped mount. Corroborated by gbhackers on the read-write host access impact. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/claude-cowork-flaw-could-let-ai-agent.html • https://gbhackers.com/claude-cowork-sandbox-flaw/
ATT&CKT1552.004 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • coworkd or the Cowork helper legitimately syncing a user-connected folder that itself happens to be ~/.aws or ~/.ssh (the user explicitly connected a credential dir)
  • Admin debugging the virtiofs mount by cat-ing a config file
  • Backup agent inside a custom image reading configs through the mount
  • Grep/find run across the whole mount for troubleshooting that incidentally matches these tokens
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName != "coworkd" and ProcessCommandLine !has "claude-cowork-helper"
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the command was NOT the user deliberately connecting a credential folder to Cowork; inspect the process lineage back to the disposable session user and any preceding pedit COW indicators. 2) Contain: kill the VM, immediately rotate the exposed SSH keys and cloud (AWS/GCP/kube) credentials, and switch the user to cloud execution. 3) Hunt: search outbound network from the guest and host for exfiltration of the harvested files, and scan other Cowork users in the fleet for the same /mnt/.virtiofs-root credential-read pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/mnt/.virtiofs-root/"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/.ssh","id_rsa","id_ed25519","/.aws","credentials","/.kube","/.config/gcloud")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "/mnt/.virtiofs-root/"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/.ssh","id_rsa","id_ed25519","/.aws","credentials","/.kube","/.config/gcloud")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
