    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |

    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic

references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1528
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate first-time SaaS app onboarding
level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",

    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04

logsource:

    product: windows

            - '\MsMpEng.exe'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")

            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:

            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.

Critical

Chaos Ransomware Uses msaRAT to Route C2 Traffic Through Headless Chrome and Edge

The Hacker News
2026-07-23 19 use cases 10 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The Chaos ransomware group ran its command-and-control through the victim's own browser. Cisco Talos on Thursday detailed msaRAT, the Rust implant behind it, found on a compromised Windows machine ahead of the encryptor. The implant never opens an outbound connection of its own. Its process talks to 127.0.0.1 and nothing else. It starts Chrome or Edge in headless mode and drives the browser

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1059.003 T1190 T1195.002 T1204.002 T1219 T1486 T1528 T1555.003 T1566
Domainsis-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev
IPs172.86.126.18
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] curl fetches fake Windows-update MSI to ProgramData from Chaos staging host · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] msaRAT command execution via cmd.exe with /e:ON /v:OFF /d /c flag combination · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Chaos Ransomware Uses msaRAT to Route C2 Traffic Through Headless Chrome and Edg
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] msiexec installs staged fake-update MSI from ProgramData (msaRAT loader) · Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Headless Chrome/Edge launched with CDP remote-debugging flags by non-interactive parent · [LLM] Browser process resolving/contacting msaRAT Cloudflare Worker C2 signaling host · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
curl fetches fake Windows-update MSI to ProgramData from Chaos staging host AIDelivery High
Hunts the msaRAT delivery step: curl.exe downloading update_ms.msi from the hard-coded staging IP 172.86.126.18 over port 443 into C:\programdata. curl writing an .msi to ProgramData from a raw IP is the article's exact loader signature and is almost never legitimate. Rationale: Anchors on the article's verbatim loader command (curl.exe, update_ms.msi, 172.86.126.18, programdata). Three independent sources (Talos, BleepingComputer, Help Net) confirm the delivery chain. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-msarat-malware-uses-chrome-edge-browsers-to-route-c2-traffic/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/cisco-talos-chaos-ransomware-msarat/
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit software packaged installers occasionally pull MSIs, but almost never via curl from a raw IP into ProgramData
  • IT automation scripts staging patches usually use a hostname + real Windows Update, not curl to a numeric IP
  • Developer testing curl against an internal artifact server (would use internal RFC1918 IP, not 172.86.126.18)
  • Security researchers detonating this exact sample in a sandbox
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\" or ProcessCommandLine has "172.86.126.18"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the download command line and whether C:\programdata\update_ms.msi landed on disk (DeviceFileEvents). Check the parent of curl.exe — a shell/RMM parent raises severity. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine/delete the MSI, and block 172.86.126.18 at the egress firewall. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for msiexec executing update_ms.msi, headless Chrome/Edge with --remote-debugging-port, and cmd.exe /e:ON /v:OFF /d /c — the downstream msaRAT stages.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "curl.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "update_ms.msi" or ProcessCommandLine has "172.86.126.18"
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"programdata"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\curl.exe"
| where CommandLine has "update_ms.msi" or CommandLine has "172.86.126.18"
| where CommandLine has "programdata"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: curl Download of Fake Windows Update MSI to ProgramData (msaRAT)
id: 8f2c1a44-6b7e-4d21-9a3c-1e5f0c9a7b21
description: Detects curl.exe fetching update_ms.msi from the Chaos/msaRAT staging IP into ProgramData
references:
  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chaos-ransomware-uses-msarat-to-route.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/23
tags:
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\curl.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: 'programdata'
  anchor:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'update_ms.msi'
      - '172.86.126.18'
  condition: selection and anchor
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\curl.exe OR *\CURL.EXE OR *\Curl.exe) (@CommandLine:*update_ms.msi* OR @CommandLine:*172.86.126.18*) @CommandLine:*programdata*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\curl\.exe$/i
| regex("programdata", field=CommandLine)
| CommandLine=/(update_ms\.msi|172\.86\.126\.18)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=curl.exe AND (Processes.process="*update_ms.msi*" OR Processes.process="*172.86.126.18*") AND Processes.process="*programdata*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=curl.exe AND (Processes.process="*update_ms.msi*" OR Processes.process="*172.86.126.18*") AND Processes.process="*programdata*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Headless Chrome/Edge launched with CDP remote-debugging flags by non-interactive parent AICommand & Control High
Hunts msaRAT's C2 transport: Chrome or Edge started with --headless=new AND --remote-debugging-port pointed at a separate --user-data-dir, spawned by an installer/service rather than a user's explorer.exe. This browser-as-C2-proxy pattern is the article's durable, technique-level signature. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim CDP launch flags (--headless=new, --remote-debugging-port) plus the article's own guidance to hunt browsers spawned by an installer/service. Talos names this the 'signal that lasts.' Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-msarat-malware-uses-chrome-edge-browsers-to-route-c2-traffic/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Puppeteer/Playwright/Selenium headless automation on developer or CI/CD hosts
  • Automated PDF/HTML-to-image rendering services that drive headless Chrome
  • Synthetic monitoring agents (e.g. uptime checks) launching headless browsers
  • Chrome/Edge enterprise printing or screenshot extensions using remote debugging
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\node_modules\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","pwsh.exe") and DeviceName !has "build"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process — legitimate CI/automation parents (node.exe, python.exe on build hosts) vs installer/service parents (msiexec.exe, services.exe, unknown binary) is the deciding factor. Confirm the --user-data-dir points to a non-standard/temp path. 2) Contain: isolate the host and suspend the parent process tree; preserve the browser user-data-dir for forensics. 3) Hunt: correlate this browser PID with loopback connections to its debugging port and outbound WebRTC to *.workers.dev / Twilio TURN; check for the curl loader and cmd.exe /e:ON /v:OFF /d /c on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--headless=new" and ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\chrome.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\msedge.exe"
| where CommandLine has "--headless=new" and CommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where ParentProcessName !endswith "\\explorer.exe" and ParentProcessName !endswith "\\chrome.exe" and ParentProcessName !endswith "\\msedge.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Headless Chrome/Edge with CDP Remote-Debugging Flags (msaRAT C2)
id: 3d9a7c15-2f88-4b6e-8c11-9a2b0e4f7d33
description: Detects Chrome or Edge launched headless with a remote-debugging port by a non-interactive parent, matching msaRAT browser-proxied C2
references:
  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/23
tags:

logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '--headless=new'
      - '--remote-debugging-port'
  filter_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\explorer.exe'
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_parent
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\chrome.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\Chrome.exe OR *\MsEdge.exe) @CommandLine:*--headless=new* @CommandLine:*--remote-debugging-port* -@ParentImage:(*\explorer.exe OR *\chrome.exe OR *\msedge.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge)\.exe$/i
| regex("--headless=new", field=CommandLine)
| regex("--remote-debugging-port", field=CommandLine)
| NOT (ParentBaseFileName=/^(explorer|chrome|msedge)\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=chrome.exe OR Processes.process_name=msedge.exe) AND Processes.process="*--headless=new*" AND Processes.process="*--remote-debugging-port*" AND Processes.parent_process_name!=explorer.exe by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=chrome.exe OR Processes.process_name=msedge.exe) AND Processes.process="*--headless=new*" AND Processes.process="*--remote-debugging-port*" AND Processes.parent_process_name!=explorer.exe by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
msaRAT command execution via cmd.exe with /e:ON /v:OFF /d /c flag combination AIExploitation Medium
Hunts msaRAT's command-execution primitive: incoming C2 frames are run through cmd.exe /e:ON /v:OFF /d /c <cmd>. This exact flag tuple (extensions on, delayed-expansion off, skip AutoRun) is a distinctive, article-specific invocation string rarely emitted by legitimate software. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim execution string 'cmd.exe /e:ON /v:OFF /d /c' from the article. The /e:ON /v:OFF /d combination together is unusual for benign automation, keeping FP low. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/
ATT&CKT1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rare legacy batch wrappers that explicitly set command extensions and disable delayed expansion
  • Some installer/uninstaller scripts that template cmd.exe with explicit /e and /v switches
  • Software build tooling that normalizes cmd invocation flags
  • Endpoint management agents (SCCM/Intune) running scripted remediations with custom cmd flags
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full command line after /c — the actual attacker command follows. Identify the parent process; a parent that also spawned headless Chrome/Edge is near-certain msaRAT. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture the process tree and the executed command for scoping, and suspend the parent implant process. 3) Hunt: pivot to the parent binary's origin (MSI custom action from C:\programdata\update_ms.msi), enumerate all commands run under this cmd tree, and check for pre-encryption discovery/recon commands preceding Chaos ransomware.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "cmd.exe"
| extend Cmd = tolower(ProcessCommandLine)
| where Cmd has "/e:on" and Cmd has "/v:off" and Cmd has "/d" and Cmd has "/c"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe"
| extend Cmd = tolower(CommandLine)
| where Cmd has "/e:on" and Cmd has "/v:off" and Cmd has "/d" and Cmd has "/c"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: cmd.exe Executed with msaRAT /e:ON /v:OFF /d /c Flag Combination
id: b71e5c2a-9d34-4f88-a1c6-2e7b0f3a9c44
description: Detects the distinctive cmd.exe flag tuple msaRAT uses to run C2-delivered commands
references:
  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/23
tags:

logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\cmd.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '/e:ON'
      - '/v:OFF'
      - '/d'
      - '/c'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\CMD.EXE OR *\Cmd.exe) @CommandLine:(*/e:ON* OR */e:on*) @CommandLine:(*/v:OFF* OR */v:off*) @CommandLine:*/d* @CommandLine:*/c*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\cmd\.exe$/i
| regex("/e:on", field=CommandLine, flags="i")
| regex("/v:off", field=CommandLine, flags="i")
| regex("/d\\b", field=CommandLine, flags="i")
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=cmd.exe AND Processes.process="*/e:ON*" AND Processes.process="*/v:OFF*" AND Processes.process="*/d*" AND Processes.process="*/c*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=cmd.exe AND Processes.process="*/e:ON*" AND Processes.process="*/v:OFF*" AND Processes.process="*/d*" AND Processes.process="*/c*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Browser process resolving/contacting msaRAT Cloudflare Worker C2 signaling host AICommand & Control High
Hunts the WebRTC signaling leg of msaRAT: a Chrome/Edge process reaching the hard-coded Cloudflare Worker is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev that brokers STUN/TURN config before relaying C2 through Twilio TURN. The specific worker hostname is the high-fidelity network anchor. Rationale: Anchors on the exact IOC hostname is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev — one of only two network indicators Talos published. Broaden to first-seen *.workers.dev per host if the operator rotates the worker. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/cisco-talos-chaos-ransomware-msarat/
ATT&CKT1102 T1090 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SaaS apps hosted on Cloudflare Workers sharing the workers.dev domain (but NOT this exact subdomain)
  • Security tooling or sandboxes replaying the IOC
  • Threat-intel enrichment platforms actively resolving the indicator
  • Note: this exact subdomain has no known benign use — a hit is high-fidelity
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is chrome.exe/msedge.exe and correlate its PID with a headless-CDP launch on the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev and global.turn.twilio.com at egress (scoped, since Twilio TURN is broadly legitimate), and terminate the browser/implant tree. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for any host resolving this worker, then broaden to first-time-seen *.workers.dev resolutions from browsers spawned by non-interactive parents.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl =~ "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name =~ "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, IPAddresses = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

msiexec installs staged fake-update MSI from ProgramData (msaRAT loader) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the install step where msiexec.exe processes C:\programdata\update_ms.msi — the fake Windows-update package whose end-of-install custom action loads the embedded msaRAT DLL (export RUN) directly into memory. An MSI executing from ProgramData is atypical of vendor installers. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim staged filename update_ms.msi and its ProgramData path. Combined they distinguish this loader from vendor MSIs that install from Temp or a signed cache. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-msarat-malware-uses-chrome-edge-browsers-to-route-c2-traffic/
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Some legitimate software caches and installs MSIs from ProgramData subfolders (e.g. certain agent updaters) — but not named update_ms.msi
  • Endpoint management (Intune/SCCM) staging MSIs in ProgramData vendor folders
  • Manual admin re-running a downloaded MSI left in ProgramData
  • AV/EDR sandbox detonation of the sample
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ccmexec.exe","intunemanagementextension.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the MSI path/name and whether it was preceded by the curl download from 172.86.126.18; inspect the MSI's ProductName/property data for Windows-update impersonation. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine update_ms.msi, and capture msiexec child processes (the in-memory DLL host). 3) Hunt: from the msiexec process tree, look for the spawned headless browser and cmd.exe /e:ON /v:OFF /d /c, and scope other hosts with the same MSI filename in ProgramData.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "update_ms.msi"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "programdata"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\msiexec.exe"
| where CommandLine has "update_ms.msi" and CommandLine has "programdata"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.005 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\outlook.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\onenote.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\mspub.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\visio.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"

status: experimental

logsource:
    category: process_creation

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/

tags:

    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'

falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

TriBack Loader DLL side-load: signed vendor EXE loading avk.dll/hostfxr.dll/MpClient.dll from user-writable path AIInstallation High
Hunts the TriBack Loader core: a legitimately-signed host binary (e.g. the renamed G DATA updater NOVupdate.exe) loading a malicious companion DLL named avk.dll, hostfxr.dll, or MpClient.dll from a user-writable, temp, or Startup directory. This is the article's primary 'detection starts with the sideloading chain' pivot and is resilient because the signed host binary rotates per build while the DLL names and file layout do not. Rationale: avk.dll is named in both Group-IB (THN) and Sophos as the sideloaded DLL; hostfxr.dll and MpClient.dll are the article's other explicitly-named side-load targets. Constraining the load path to user-writable dirs removes legitimate framework DLLs in System32/Program Files. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/donuts-and-beagles-fake-claude-site-spreads-backdoor • https://cyberpress.org/jadeprox-triback-campaign/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-claude-ai-website-delivers-new-beagle-windows-malware/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate .NET apps loading a genuine hostfxr.dll from a self-contained deployment unpacked into %TEMP% or AppData
  • Portable/ClickOnce applications that ship hostfxr.dll in AppData\Local
  • G DATA / other AV product legitimately writing avk.dll or MpClient.dll into its own ProgramData install path
  • Developer build output directories under user profiles containing hostfxr.dll
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Program Files\" and FileName =~ "hostfxr.dll")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the loading process (InitiatingProcessFileName/FolderPath) and its digital signature — a signed vendor EXE running from AppData/Temp/Startup with these DLLs beside an encrypted .dat/.log is the loader. Check for a NOVupdate.exe.dat companion. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the host-binary process tree, and quarantine the DLL + .dat/.log companion; block outbound to the campaign C2 (see C2 UC). 3) Hunt: sweep the estate for the same DLL names in user-writable paths, for ~del.vbs.bat and _CL_###### folders, and for Startup-folder persistence dropped by an MSI.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("avk.dll","hostfxr.dll","MpClient.dll")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\ProgramData\")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\ProgramData\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, HostBinary = InitiatingProcessFileName, HostPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, LoadedDll = FileName, DllPath = FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("avk.dll","hostfxr.dll","MpClient.dll")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\ProgramData\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: TriBack Loader Sideloaded DLL In User-Writable Path
id: 7c9a1e42-3b6d-4f2a-9c11-2d5e8f0a4b71
description: Malicious companion DLL (avk.dll/hostfxr.dll/MpClient.dll) loaded from a user-writable, temp, or Startup directory by a signed host binary (TriBack Loader).
references:

  - https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/donuts-and-beagles-fake-claude-site-spreads-backdoor

date: 2026/07/23

#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\(avk|hostfxr|MpClient)\.dll$/i | regex("\\\\(AppData|Temp|Startup|Public|ProgramData)\\\\", field=TargetFileName) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT

TriBack Loader Startup-folder persistence: signed EXE + encrypted .dat/.log + malicious DLL trio dropped by MSI AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence stage where the Claude-themed MSI installer (post-UAC) drops the full sideloading chain into the Windows Startup folder: a signed host binary, an encrypted .dat/.log payload, and a malicious DLL (observed: NOVupdate.exe + NOVupdate.exe.dat + avk.dll). Also flags the campaign's cleanup/staging artifacts ~del.vbs.bat and nested _CL_###### folders. Rationale: Sophos confirms the MSI drops NOVupdate.exe + NOVupdate.exe.dat + avk.dll into the user's Startup folder; the article adds ~del.vbs.bat and _CL_###### folders. Encrypted .dat/.log beside an executable in Startup is the article's stated highest-fidelity file-layout tell. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/donuts-and-beagles-fake-claude-site-spreads-backdoor • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-claude-ai-website-delivers-new-beagle-windows-malware/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate installers placing an app shortcut/EXE in the Startup folder (though .dat/.log companions are unusual)
  • OneDrive/Teams/Slack auto-launch stubs written to Startup on first login
  • Backup/sync tools staging temporary .log files that briefly appear in the Startup path
  • Antivirus updaters (G DATA) legitimately writing avk.dll to their real ProgramData install directory rather than Startup
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe") or FileName in~ ("NOVupdate.exe","NOVupdate.exe.dat","avk.dll","~del.vbs.bat")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process — an MSI/msiexec.exe or a browser-spawned installer writing a signed EXE + .dat + .dll trio into Startup is the loader; validate the EXE's signature and whether the .dat XORs to shellcode. 2) Contain: remove the Startup-folder entries, isolate the host, and disable the auto-run; capture the .dat/.log and DLL for reversing. 3) Hunt: pivot to the DLL side-load UC on the same host, check DNS/proxy for licence.claude-pro.com and the other campaign domains, and search other endpoints for identical Startup-folder trios.
let StartupPath = @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\";
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where (FolderPath has StartupPath and (FileName endswith ".dat" or FileName endswith ".log" or FileName endswith ".dll" or FileName endswith ".exe"))
     or FileName in~ ("NOVupdate.exe","NOVupdate.exe.dat","avk.dll","~del.vbs.bat")
     or FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)\\_CL_[0-9]{6}\\"
| summarize DroppedFiles = make_set(FileName, 20), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), FileCount = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where FileCount >= 1
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where (TargetFilePath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\" and (TargetFileName endswith ".dat" or TargetFileName endswith ".log" or TargetFileName endswith ".dll" or TargetFileName endswith ".exe"))
     or TargetFileName in~ ("NOVupdate.exe","NOVupdate.exe.dat","avk.dll","~del.vbs.bat")
     or TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)\\_CL_[0-9]{6}\\"
| summarize DroppedFiles = make_set(TargetFileName, 20), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| order by FirstSeen desc

JadeProx / Beagle C2 to campaign domains and 43.106.71.28:8000 staging server AICommand & Control Medium
Detects endpoint communication with the JadeProx cluster infrastructure: the Beagle C2 licence/license.claude-pro.com (TCP 443 / UDP 8080), the other campaign domains, and the staging server 43.106.71.28 on port 8000. Covers both DNS resolution and direct-IP connections so it fires whether the host resolves a domain or beacons to a hard-coded IP. Rationale: Every domain/IP is from Group-IB's July 23 IOC block; Sophos independently confirms licence.claude-pro.com as the Beagle C2 (TCP443/UDP8080) and 43.106.71.28:8000 as the staging server. Both spellings license/licence are included because Sophos and the article differ. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/donuts-and-beagles-fake-claude-site-spreads-backdoor • https://cyberpress.org/jadeprox-triback-campaign/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1095 T1573.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/malware analysts or sandboxes deliberately resolving these IOC domains during research
  • Security tooling that pre-resolves IOC feeds for enrichment (SOAR, TIP connectors) generating benign DNS to the domains
  • A user genuinely fooled by malvertising resolving claude-pro.com — this is a true positive, not an FP, and should be triaged as compromise
  • Corporate proxy logging the same DNS twice (endpoint + proxy) causing duplicate alerts
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","MsMpEng.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — a browser resolving claude-pro.com is malvertising victim; a NOVupdate.exe/renamed signed binary beaconing to licence.claude-pro.com:443 or 43.106.71.28:8000 is active Beagle C2. 2) Contain: block the domains/IPs at proxy+firewall, isolate the beaconing host, and reset credentials used on it. 3) Hunt: pull the sideloading-chain and Startup-persistence UCs for the same DeviceName, and sweep DNS/proxy org-wide for any other host that resolved these domains in the last 30 days.
let CampaignDomains = dynamic(["claude-pro.com","license.claude-pro.com","licence.claude-pro.com","sylverixstrategy.com","gouvvbo.top","vertextrust-advisors.com","update-trellix.com","update-crowdstrike.com","update-sentinelone.com"]);
let CampaignIPs = dynamic(["43.106.71.28","8.217.190.58","209.189.190.206","178.128.108.89","192.252.186.62"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)

Fake Claude malvertising: MSI/ZIP download originating from claude-pro.com AIDelivery High
Detects the initial-access vector — a host downloading an installer (MSI) or large ZIP archive whose file-origin URL is the fake Claude site claude-pro.com (the ~505 MB 'Claude-Pro Relay' lure served via search malvertising). This catches victims before the loader chain executes. Rationale: Sophos confirms claude-pro.com served a ~505 MB ZIP containing the MSI (renamed G DATA updater side-load chain) and assesses it as active malvertising; FileOriginUrl anchoring on claude-pro.com catches the download before execution and is a distinct pivot from live C2. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/donuts-and-beagles-fake-claude-site-spreads-backdoor • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-claude-ai-website-delivers-new-beagle-windows-malware/
ATT&CKT1189 T1204.002
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A researcher intentionally downloading the sample from claude-pro.com in a sandbox
  • Web-content proxies pre-fetching the URL for inspection and logging a synthetic download
  • Browser caching artifacts recording claude-pro.com as origin without a completed download
  • Any hit here is high-confidence malicious — claude-pro.com is not a legitimate Anthropic domain (real domain is claude.ai)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the download completed and whether the MSI/ZIP was executed (pivot to msiexec.exe and the Startup-folder UC on the same host). 2) Contain: block claude-pro.com at web proxy, delete the downloaded archive, and isolate the host if the installer ran. 3) Hunt: search org-wide for any other endpoint with a claude-pro.com file origin, and for the sideloading DLL/Startup artifacts that follow execution.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where isnotempty(FileOriginUrl) and FileOriginUrl has "claude-pro.com"
| where FileName endswith ".msi" or FileName endswith ".zip" or FileName endswith ".exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginIP, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RequestURL has "claude-pro.com"
| where RequestURL has_any (".msi", ".zip", "Claude-Pro", "Relay") or tostring(ReceivedBytes) matches regex @"\d{9,}"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceHostName, SourceUserName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, ReceivedBytes, DestinationHostName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Internet-facing hosts exposed to the four CVEs JadeProx actively scanned/exploited AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces assets vulnerable to the exact four 9.8-rated CVEs the JadeProx operators ran Nuclei critical-severity templates for and attempted against individual hosts: CVE-2018-11511 (ASUSTOR ADM), CVE-2021-24139 (10Web Photo Gallery WP plugin), CVE-2021-31755 (Tenda AC11), and CVE-2021-32305 (WebSVN). Prioritises patching/isolation of the exact break-in surface, with the CISA-KEV Tenda bug ranked first. Rationale: The four CVEs and their 9.8 scores are named verbatim in the article and confirmed against NVD by THN; CVE-2021-31755 is called out as CISA-KEV. This is an exposure hunt against the exact break-in surface rather than a generic critical-vuln sweep. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/china-nexus-jadeprox-uses-new-triback.html • https://cyberpress.org/jadeprox-triback-campaign/
ATT&CKT1190 T1595.002
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Isolated/lab appliances that carry the vulnerable firmware but are not internet-reachable (deprioritise, not dismiss)
  • TVM version-inference false matches on repackaged/backported firmware where the fix was applied without a version bump
  • Decommissioned assets still present in the TVM inventory
  • Third-party managed appliances (ASUSTOR NAS, Tenda routers) outside the patch mandate but still on the network
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank hits by IsInternetFacing then by CVE-2021-31755 (CISA-KEV, remediation deadline long expired); confirm exposed service/port for each asset. 2) Contain: patch or take offline the internet-facing vulnerable hosts first; put a WAF/ACL in front of any that cannot be patched immediately. 3) Hunt: on any vulnerable internet-facing host, check web/app logs for Nuclei-style scanning and exploitation, and for webshells on exposed Java management interfaces (the article's stated entry method), then pivot to the C2 and sideloading UCs.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
