| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=chrome.exe OR Processes.process_name=msedge.exe) (Processes.process="*--remote-debugging-port*" OR Processes.process="*--headless*") NOT (Processes.parent_process_name IN (explorer.exe,chrome.exe,msedge.exe,msedgewebview2.exe,userinit.exe)) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=chrome.exe OR Processes.process_name=msedge.exe) (Processes.process="*--remote-debugging-port*" OR Processes.process="*--headless*") NOT (Processes.parent_process_name IN (explorer.exe,chrome.exe,msedge.exe,msedgewebview2.exe,userinit.exe)) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
msaRAT C2 network IOC: connection to 172.86.126.18 or is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts network contact with the hardcoded Chaos/msaRAT infrastructure — the delivery IP 172.86.126.18 and the Cloudflare Workers signaling endpoint is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev used for SDP/ICE exchange. Pure IOC pivot corroborated by Talos. Rationale: Both the delivery IP 172.86.126.18 and the Cloudflare Workers signaling domain are verbatim, campaign-unique IOCs from the Talos article; direct network matches are the highest-fidelity possible pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://malware.news/t/chaos-ransomwares-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-a-covert-c2-channel/124199
ATT&CKT1102 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate host also using an unrelated *.workers.dev service (mitigated by the exact subdomain match)
  • Threat-intel sandbox / detonation VM deliberately contacting the IOC
  • Security scanner probing the attacker IP
  • Proxy log replay from an IR investigation
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the source host and the initiating process (a browser process for the workers.dev signaling, or curl/msiexec for the delivery IP). 2. Contain: block 172.86.126.18 and is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev at the firewall/proxy and network-isolate the source host. 3. Hunt: on the host, look back for the curl download of update_ms.msi, msiexec execution, headless browser launch with CDP flags, RMM tooling, and outbound Twilio TURN (global.turn.twilio.com) traffic indicating the WebRTC DataChannel is live.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "172.86.126.18" or RemoteUrl has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "172.86.126.18" or DestinationHostName =~ "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev" or RequestURL has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationPort, RequestURL, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

New msaRAT malware uses Chrome, Edge browsers to route C2 traffic

BleepingComputer
2026-07-23 14 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The Chaos ransomware gang is using a new backdoor dubbed msaRAT that hides command-and-control (C2) communication by routing it through the Chrome or Edge browsers. [...]

ATT&CKT1190 T1486 T1566
Domainsis-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev
IPs172.86.126.18
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] MSI masquerading as Windows Update (update_ms.msi) delivering msaRAT lib.dll · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — New msaRAT malware uses Chrome, Edge browsers to route C2 traffic
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Headless Chrome/Edge launched with remote-debugging by anomalous parent (msaRAT CDP C2 setup)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Browser contacting msaRAT Cloudflare Workers signaling host / staging IP · [LLM] Non-browser process connecting to localhost DevTools debug port (msaRAT loopback CDP control) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Headless Chrome/Edge launched with remote-debugging by anomalous parent (msaRAT CDP C2 setup) AIInstallation High
Hunts msaRAT (lib.dll) launching a user-installed Chrome or Edge in headless mode with the remote-debugging interface enabled so it can drive the browser over Chrome DevTools Protocol. The combination of --headless plus --remote-debugging-port/-pipe spawned by a non-launcher parent is the browser-hijack initialization step that precedes all C2. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's execution primitive ('launches the browser in headless mode... enables the browser's remote debugging interface and connects to it via CDP'). --headless + --remote-debugging together, minus normal automation/launcher parents, is a rare, high-fidelity pair. Corroborated by Talos and The Hacker News write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chaos-ransomware-uses-msarat-to-route.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/cisco-talos-chaos-ransomware-msarat/
ATT&CKT1564.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Puppeteer/Playwright/Selenium automation launched by node.exe or python.exe (excluded by parent filter but bespoke wrappers may slip through)
  • Synthetic web monitoring / uptime agents that headless-render pages
  • PDF-generation services (e.g. headless Chrome print-to-PDF) run by a backend service account
  • Security scanners / DAST tools that drive a headless browser
  • Internal RPA tooling that scripts a browser via CDP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\node_modules\\" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "puppeteer" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "playwright"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and the parent lineage — confirm the parent is not a sanctioned automation host (node/python/CI agent) and capture the remote-debugging port value from the command line. Check whether an interactive user session exists on the host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the headless browser and its parent process tree, and block outbound to is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev and 172.86.126.18. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for update_ms.msi / lib.dll, a non-browser process connecting to 127.0.0.1 on the debug port, and subsequent traffic to *.workers.dev / Twilio TURN infrastructure.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--headless"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port","--remote-debugging-pipe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","userinit.exe","node.exe","python.exe","java.exe","electron.exe","code.exe","chromedriver.exe","msedgedriver.exe","msedgewebview2.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--headless"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port","--remote-debugging-pipe")
| where not(ParentProcessName has_any ("explorer.exe","userinit.exe","node.exe","python.exe","java.exe","electron.exe","code.exe","chromedriver.exe","msedgedriver.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Browser contacting msaRAT Cloudflare Workers signaling host / staging IP AICommand & Control High
Alerts on any endpoint resolving or connecting to the msaRAT signaling endpoint is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev or the staging IP 172.86.126.18. The browser fetches WebRTC connection info from this Cloudflare Worker to bootstrap the encrypted C2 channel, making the host a direct named IOC. Rationale: Uses the two confirmed network IOCs from Talos' IOC repo (the only published indicators): signaling host is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev and staging IP 172.86.126.18. Both are unique, so any match is high-fidelity despite the workers.dev parent domain being shared with benign deployments. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/cisco-talos-chaos-ransomware-msarat/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal app genuinely hosted on the same specific Worker subdomain (extremely unlikely given the random-looking name)
  • Threat-intel enrichment / sandbox detonation host deliberately resolving the IOC
  • Security researcher or IR analyst manually browsing to the IOC during investigation
  • Shared-egress NAT attributing the resolution to the wrong internal host (verify the true source via endpoint DNS)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the true source host and the process that initiated the resolution/connection (chrome.exe/msedge.exe expected). Confirm whether a headless browser with remote-debugging was launched on that host in the preceding minutes. 2) Contain: isolate the host and block is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev and 172.86.126.18 at DNS/proxy/firewall. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for the same IOC, look for update_ms.msi / lib.dll and headless-browser launches, and pivot on outbound WebRTC/TURN traffic from browser processes.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev" or RemoteIP == "172.86.126.18"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationHostName has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev" or RequestURL has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev" or DestinationIP == "172.86.126.18"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DestinationIP, DestinationPort
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MSI masquerading as Windows Update (update_ms.msi) delivering msaRAT lib.dll AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the msaRAT delivery step where msiexec executes an installer named to look like a Windows update (update_ms.msi) that loads lib.dll into memory. Scopes to msiexec invocations with update-style MSI naming spawned outside legitimate patching channels (WU/SCCM/TrustedInstaller). Rationale: Anchors on the corroborated filename update_ms.msi (surfaced in Talos coverage / Help Net Security) and the article's statement that the MSI 'posing as a Windows update' loads lib.dll in memory. Parent exclusions strip legitimate WU/SCCM/TrustedInstaller patching to keep the update-style naming heuristic usable. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/cisco-talos-chaos-ransomware-msarat/
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1036.005 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party software updaters that name their MSI packages with 'update' or version/KB strings and run outside SCCM
  • Admin-driven manual patch installs from a network share or Downloads folder
  • Vendor agent self-update MSIs (e.g. driver/firmware update packages) launched by a helper service not in the exclusion list
  • Software packaging/test labs building MSIs named update*.msi
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\ccmcache\\" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "\\SoftwareDistribution\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the referenced .msi and check signer — a Microsoft-signed, WU-catalogued update is benign; an unsigned/unknown signer named like an update is not. Review parent process and how the MSI reached the host (email attachment, RMM push, share). 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the MSI and any dropped lib.dll, and terminate any headless browser processes. 3) Hunt: search for lib.dll image loads into non-standard hosts, headless Chrome/Edge with remote-debugging, and connections to the workers.dev signaling host across the fleet.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "update_ms.msi"
    or (ProcessCommandLine has ".msi" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("update","KB","patch") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/i","/quiet","/qn"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("services.exe","ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe","wuauclt.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","msiexec.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "msiexec.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "update_ms.msi" or (ActingProcessCommandLine has ".msi" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("update","KB","patch"))
| where not(ParentProcessName has_any ("services.exe","ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","wuauclt.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: MSI Masquerading as Windows Update - msaRAT update_ms.msi

Non-browser process connecting to localhost DevTools debug port (msaRAT loopback CDP control) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the msaRAT control channel where a non-browser process connects only to 127.0.0.1 to drive the headless browser over Chrome DevTools Protocol. Talos notes the implant 'talks to 127.0.0.1 and nothing else' — a non-browser initiator reaching the loopback DevTools port range is anomalous local-IPC-for-C2 behaviour. Rationale: Encodes Talos' distinguishing detail that the implant only ever talks to 127.0.0.1 and drives the browser over CDP. Scoping to the documented DevTools port range (9222-9299) with a non-browser initiator surfaces the loopback control channel; note the debug port is configurable, so pair with UC1 which reveals the actual port from the command line. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chaos-ransomware-uses-msarat-to-route.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer or QA machines running Puppeteer/Playwright/Selenium where the driver connects to the browser debug port (partially excluded by process filter)
  • IDE/editor debug integrations (VS Code, JetBrains) attaching to a Chromium debug port
  • Electron apps or embedded-browser tooling using CDP locally
  • Web performance/lighthouse tooling connecting to a local headless browser
  • Loopback IPC on 9222-9299 by unrelated apps that happen to use those ports
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\node_modules\\" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("puppeteer","playwright","lighthouse","selenium")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process image and command line — confirm it is not a sanctioned dev/automation tool, and check whether a headless Chrome/Edge with remote-debugging was launched on the host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the initiating process and the headless browser tree, and block the workers.dev signaling host and staging IP. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 (headless launch) and UC2 (workers.dev egress) on the same DeviceId, and search for update_ms.msi / lib.dll to confirm the full msaRAT chain.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| where RemotePort between (9222 .. 9299)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","node.exe","code.exe","msedgewebview2.exe","chromedriver.exe","msedgedriver.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| where RemotePort between (9222 .. 9299)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","node.exe","code.exe","msedgewebview2.exe","chromedriver.exe","msedgedriver.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc

| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental

Check Point Patches Exploited SmartConsole Flaw Allowing Full Admin Access

The Hacker NewsBleepingComputer
2026-07-23 18 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Check Point has released security updates to address multiple vulnerabilities impacting Security Management and Multi-Domain Management (MDSM) products, including a critical flaw that has come under active exploitation in the wild. The security flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-16232 (CVSS score: 9.3), is an authentication bypass affecting the Check Point SmartConsole login process that allows an

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Exposure inventory: unpatched Check Point Management on vulnerable R77.30-R82.10 builds · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound connections from CVE-2026-16232 exploitation IPs to Check Point Management Server · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] CVE-2026-16232 SmartConsole auth bypass via application-token login · [LLM] Gaia Portal read-only user executing root-level commands (CVE-2026-62145) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] New Check Point administrator account or role grant after management compromise · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Check Point Management run-script / exec-command execution on Security Gateway (CVE-2026-62144) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Inbound connections from CVE-2026-16232 exploitation IPs to Check Point Management Server AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for network sessions to/from the six attacker IPs Check Point published for the in-the-wild CVE-2026-16232 SmartConsole authentication-bypass campaign. Fires on any org host (especially an internet-exposed Security Management / MDSM server) talking to this infrastructure. Rationale: Uses the six exact IOC IPs Check Point published for the actively-exploited CVE-2026-16232 campaign; any contact with this infrastructure is high-fidelity because these are dedicated attacker nodes, not shared cloud ranges.
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel platform or security scanner sinkholing/validating the same IPs from a monitored host
  • SOC analyst manually curling an IOC IP during triage
  • Passive DNS / IOC-enrichment appliance beaconing to reputation services that proxy these IPs
  • An IP later re-provisioned to a benign hosting tenant after takedown
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nessus.exe","scanner.exe") or DeviceName has_any ("vulnscan","threatintel"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the local host and, if it is a Check Point Management/MDSM server, treat as likely-compromised; pull the session direction (inbound to 19009/18190/443 = exploitation attempt, outbound = possible C2). 2) Contain: block the six IOC IPs at the perimeter, restrict Trusted Clients to management subnets, and isolate the management host if inbound admin sessions from these IPs succeeded. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source/dest host for SmartConsole admin logins, run-script/exec-command audit entries, and new administrator objects within the same window.

CVE-2026-16232 SmartConsole auth bypass via application-token login AIExploitation Medium
Detects the CVE-2026-16232 authentication-bypass pattern: a successful SmartConsole administrator authentication to the Security Management / MDSM server originating from an external (non-RFC1918, non-allowlisted) source, which is exactly the 'Management exposed to the internet without IP restrictions' precondition Check Point named. Also flags admin logins sourced from the six published IOC IPs. Rationale: Grounded in Check Point's stated precondition — 'Management exposed directly to the internet without IP restrictions' — so an admin/CPMI session from a public source on the management ports is the exploitation signature; IOC-IP enrichment raises it to alerting fidelity.
ATT&CKT1190 T1548 T1078
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote administrator connecting to SmartConsole over the internet without a VPN (poor-but-real practice)
  • Managed-service-provider (MSP) managing the Check Point estate from their own public egress IP
  • Third-party monitoring appliance polling the management API over 443
  • NAT/proxy collapsing internal admin traffic to a public-looking egress address
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<known-msp-egress-not-applicable>") and not(SourceUserName in~ ("svc-monitoring"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the successful admin session's SourceIP is on the Trusted Clients allowlist and whether it matches a known admin/MSP; cross-check against the six IOC IPs. 2) Contain: force-restrict Trusted Clients to management subnets, rotate all SmartConsole admin credentials/API keys, and terminate active external management sessions. 3) Hunt: for any confirmed external admin login, enumerate subsequent run-script/exec-command operations, policy pushes, and new administrator objects created by that session.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where LocalPort in (19009, 18190, 443)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let iocs = dynamic(["151.241.99.207","151.241.99.233","158.62.198.182","192.142.10.99","139.28.37.250","194.213.18.137"]);
CommonSecurityLog

| where DeviceVendor has "Check Point"
| where Activity has_any ("Log In","Login","Administrator login","authentication","session") or DeviceAction has_any ("login","authenticate")
| where isnotempty(SourceIP)
| extend IsIoc = SourceIP in (iocs)
| where IsIoc or not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, AccountName, Activity, DeviceAction, IsIoc, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Check Point Management run-script / exec-command execution on Security Gateway (CVE-2026-62144) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the CVE-2026-62144 post-exploitation action: an unauthenticated attacker abusing the Management Server to run administrative commands (run-script, exec-command) against Security Gateways. Surfaces these command operations in Check Point management audit logs, prioritising sessions from external/IOC sources. Rationale: Uses the two administrative command primitives (run-script, exec-command) named verbatim in the article for CVE-2026-62144; their appearance in management audit — especially tied to an external/IOC source — is the concrete post-exploitation action.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059 T1219
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate administrator pushing a maintenance script to gateways via SmartConsole run-script
  • Automation/orchestration (Ansible, cpmi API) issuing exec-command as part of change management
  • Check Point Professional Services performing a health check
  • Scheduled config-audit jobs that shell out to gateways
Suppression filter
| where not (SourceUserName in~ ("svc-automation","ansible") and ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating admin/session and SourceIP for each run-script/exec-command event; confirm it corresponds to an approved change ticket and an internal/allowlisted source. 2) Contain: if the source is external/IOC or unattributed, suspend the admin account, revoke API sessions, and freeze policy installation while you capture the exact command bodies from the audit Message. 3) Hunt: recover the executed scripts, check gateways for dropped files/new listeners/altered rulebases, and correlate with CVE-2026-16232 admin-login events from the same source.

| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, AccountName, Activity, DeviceAction, IsIoc, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New Check Point administrator account or role grant after management compromise AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for creation of a new administrator object or elevation of a role within Check Point management following CVE-2026-16232 full-admin access — a backdoor-persistence step. Prioritises admin-object changes made from external or IOC-linked sessions. Rationale: Full-admin access from CVE-2026-16232 lets the attacker mint durable admin backdoors; administrator-object creation/role-grant events in Check Point audit are the concrete persistence artifact, IOC-source-enriched to cut noise.
ATT&CKT1078 T1098 T1136
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Onboarding a legitimate new firewall administrator during normal IAM lifecycle
  • MSP adding a scoped admin for a new engagement
  • Role adjustment during a planned RBAC re-org
  • Automated provisioning creating service admins for API integrations
Suppression filter
| where not (SourceUserName in~ ("iam-provisioning","svc-onboard") and ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each new/elevated administrator, verify an approved onboarding/change ticket and that the creating session came from an internal, allowlisted source (not IOC/external). 2) Contain: disable and quarantine any unattributed admin account, revoke its API keys/sessions, and force MFA + password reset on all remaining admins. 3) Hunt: review everything that account did (policy pushes, run-script/exec-command, object edits) and correlate its creation timestamp against CVE-2026-16232 external admin logins.
let iocs = dynamic(["151.241.99.207","151.241.99.233","158.62.198.182","192.142.10.99","139.28.37.250","194.213.18.137"]);
CommonSecurityLog

| where DeviceVendor has "Check Point"
| where Activity has_any ("add-administrator","Create Administrator","administrator","set-administrator","add admin") and Activity has_any ("add","create","set","grant") 
| extend IsIoc = SourceIP in (iocs)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, AccountName, Activity, DeviceAction, IsIoc, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gaia Portal read-only user executing root-level commands (CVE-2026-62145) AIExploitation Low
Hunts the CVE-2026-62145 improper-privilege-management flaw where an authenticated read-only Gaia Portal user executes commands with root privileges. Surfaces privileged command execution on the Gaia appliance attributed to a non-admin/read-only role. Rationale: Maps directly to CVE-2026-62145's described behaviour — a read-only Gaia Portal user gaining root command execution; low confidence because the article gives no exact log string, so this is a hunting query on Gaia syslog role+privilege mismatch.
ATT&CKT1068 T1548
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin whose role was recently upgraded but still tagged read-only in cached logs
  • Support engineer legitimately entering expert mode with proper privileges (mis-parsed role field)
  • Backup/monitoring account intentionally granted limited expert access
  • Log-parsing artifact where the role field and command field are misaligned
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the acting account's actual Gaia role is read-only/monitor and that it truly executed a root/expert command (not a mis-parsed field). 2) Contain: apply the July 22 Jumbo hotfix on the affected Gaia appliance, revoke the read-only account's access, and audit its recent command history for config tampering. 3) Hunt: check whether the same account or source also triggered CVE-2026-16232/62144 activity and inspect the gateway for persistence (new services, cron, modified rulebases).

| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, Facility, SeverityLevel, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exposure inventory: unpatched Check Point Management on vulnerable R77.30-R82.10 builds AIReconnaissance High
Identifies Security Management / MDSM / Gaia assets still carrying CVE-2026-16232, CVE-2026-62144, or CVE-2026-62145 (all three impact R77.30 through R82.10) so the SOC can drive the CISA-KEV-mandated July 22 Jumbo hotfix before internet exposure is exploited. Rationale: Uses the three exact CVE IDs and the R77.30-R82.10 affected-version range stated in the article plus CISA KEV's July 25 remediation deadline; joining to DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing prioritises the exact 'Management exposed to the internet' configuration Check Point flagged as the exploit precondition.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM scanner reporting a version that has already had the Jumbo hotfix applied out-of-band (stale inventory)
  • Lab/decommissioned management appliance flagged but not in production
  • Third-party product string collision matching Check Point CVE IDs
  • Asset behind additional compensating controls (Trusted Clients already restricted) still flagged as vulnerable
Suppression filter
| where RecommendedSecurityUpdate != "" and isnotempty(SoftwareVersion)
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank flagged assets by IsInternetFacing/PublicIP and role (Management/MDSM first); confirm current build vs the July 22 Jumbo hotfix baseline. 2) Contain: for any internet-facing management host, immediately restrict Trusted Clients to trusted subnets and place management behind the firewall as an interim control, then schedule the hotfix. 3) Hunt: on every exposed-and-vulnerable host, run the IOC-IP, external-admin-login, and run-script/exec-command detections to rule out prior exploitation before closing the ticket.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Web

| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

     | rename recipient AS recipient]

    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count

    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

CloudAppEvents

| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Shai-Hulud / GhostAction malicious workflow artifact dropped on runner or repo checkout
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network egress from CI/build host to GhostAction secret-exfil infrastructure · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] CI runner process POSTing secrets to GhostAction exfil host via curl/wget/node · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Network egress from CI/build host to GhostAction secret-exfil infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections from self-hosted GitHub Actions runners (or any host) to the GhostAction campaign's exfiltration infrastructure — the 45.139.104.115 / 216.126.225.129 IPs and the bold-dhawan/objective-hopper .plesk.page and carte-avantage.com domains that received 3,325+ stolen Actions secrets via curl POST. Pure IOC match on confirmed campaign infra, so any hit is a near-certain secret-dump in flight. Rationale: Uses the article's pre-extracted GhostAction IPs (45.139.104.115, 216.126.225.129) and domains (bold-dhawan/objective-hopper.plesk.page, carte-avantage.com), all independently confirmed by GitGuardian/BleepingComputer as the campaign's secret-exfil endpoints — hard IOCs, near-zero benign contact. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.gitguardian.com/ghostaction-campaign-3-325-secrets-stolen/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-steal-3-325-secrets-in-ghostaction-github-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/ghostaction-campaign-over-3-000-secrets-stolen-through-malicious-github-workflows
ATT&CKT1567 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or malware sandbox intentionally connecting to the IOC hosts for validation
  • Threat-intel enrichment/beaconing-check tooling that resolves or pings known-bad domains
  • Firewall logging a blocked/denied connection attempt (still worth reviewing, not a true compromise)
  • A future benign tenant reusing the 45-139-104-115.plesk.page shared-hosting range after takedown
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","MsMpEng.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host — confirm whether it is a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner or CI build agent; pull the initiating process and command line. 2) Contain: block the IOC IPs/domains at egress, isolate the runner, and immediately rotate every secret that runner had access to (npm/PyPI/DockerHub/cloud tokens). 3) Hunt: enumerate all repos whose workflows executed on that runner, review recent .github/workflows commits for injected exfil steps, and pivot to UC2/UC3 on the same host.
let iocIPs = dynamic(["45.139.104.115","216.126.225.129"]);
let iocDomains = dynamic(["bold-dhawan.45-139-104-115.plesk.page","objective-hopper.45-139-104-115.plesk.page","carte-avantage.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (iocIPs) or RemoteUrl has_any (iocDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

union isfuzzy=true

 | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DeviceProduct),
(DnsEvents
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where Name has_any (iocDomains)
 | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
